title: Question 4
stem:
Two vertical metal plates in a vacuum are separated by a distance of $0.12\text{m}$. Fig. 4.1 shows a side view of this arrangement.

{{figure:figure_4_1}}

Fig. 4.1 (not to scale)

Each plate has a length of $2.0\text{m}$. The potential difference between the plates is $900\text{V}$. The electric field between the plates is uniform.

A negatively charged sand particle is released from rest at point X, which is a horizontal distance of $0.080\text{m}$ from the top of the positively charged plate. The particle then travels in a straight line and collides with the positively charged plate at its lowest point Y, as illustrated in Fig. 4.1.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Describe the pattern of the field lines (lines of force) between the plates.

markscheme_points.text: straight (horizontal) lines and from the +0.90 kV plate/to the 0 V plate

hints: Parallel plates produce a uniform field, so consider both the shape and spacing of the field lines.
The field lines are perpendicular to the vertical plates and point from the +900 V plate toward the 0 V plate.
walkthrough: A uniform electric field has field lines that are straight and parallel, with equal spacing between neighbouring lines.
The field is perpendicular to the vertical plates, so the lines are horizontal.
Electric field direction is from higher positive potential to lower potential: from the +900 V plate to the 0 V plate.

hints: Parallel plates produce a uniform field, so consider both the shape and spacing of the field lines.
The field lines are perpendicular to the vertical plates and point from the +900 V plate toward the 0 V plate.
walkthrough: A uniform electric field has field lines that are straight and parallel, with equal spacing between neighbouring lines.
The field is perpendicular to the vertical plates, so the lines are horizontal.
Electric field direction is from higher positive potential to lower potential: from the +900 V plate to the 0 V plate.

ai_rubric.observable: Describes straight horizontal field lines directed from the +900 V plate to the 0 V plate.
States that the field lines are equally spaced.

marking_points.text: straight (horizontal) lines and from the +0.90 kV plate/to the 0 V plate

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: State the names of the two forces acting on the particle as it moves from X to Y.
hints: The particle is in an electric field but it also has mass, so identify one interaction associated with each fact.
Think about the force caused by an electric field on charge, and the force caused by gravity on mass.
walkthrough: A charged particle in an electric field experiences an electric force.
Because the particle has mass and is near the Earth, it also experiences its weight, the gravitational force.
The two forces are electric force and weight.

ai_rubric.observable: Names both the electric force and the weight, or gravitational force, acting on the particle.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: By considering the vertical motion of the sand particle, show that the time taken for the particle to move from X to Y is $0.64\text{s}$.

markscheme_points.text: s = 1/2 at^2 or s = ut + 1/2 at^2 and u = 0

hints: For the vertical motion, the particle starts from rest and accelerates downward at g over the 2.0 m plate length.
Set s = ½at² with s = 2.0 m and a = 9.81 m s⁻², then solve for t.
walkthrough: The particle is released from rest, so its initial vertical velocity is u = 0.
Its vertical motion has constant acceleration g = 9.81 m s⁻² over a displacement of 2.0 m.
Use s = ut + ½at², giving 2.0 = ½(9.81)t².
The time taken is 0.64 s.

hints: For the vertical motion, the particle starts from rest and accelerates downward at g over the 2.0 m plate length.
Set s = ½at² with s = 2.0 m and a = 9.81 m s⁻², then solve for t.
walkthrough: The particle is released from rest, so its initial vertical velocity is u = 0.
Its vertical motion has constant acceleration g = 9.81 m s⁻² over a displacement of 2.0 m.
Use s = ut + ½at², giving 2.0 = ½(9.81)t².
The time taken is 0.64 s.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses s = ½at², or s = ut + ½at² with u = 0, for the vertical motion.
Substitutes 2.0 = ½(9.81)t² and obtains 0.64 s.

marking_points.text: s = 1/2 at^2 or s = ut + 1/2 at^2 and u = 0

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Calculate the horizontal component of the acceleration of the particle.
hints: The particle starts from rest horizontally and covers 0.080 m in the time found for the vertical motion.
Use 0.080 = ½a(0.64)² and rearrange for the horizontal acceleration.
walkthrough: Horizontally, the particle starts from rest and moves 0.080 m in 0.64 s.
Use s = ½at²: 0.080 = ½a(0.64)².
The horizontal component of acceleration is 0.39 m s⁻².

hints: The particle starts from rest horizontally and covers 0.080 m in the time found for the vertical motion.
Use 0.080 = ½a(0.64)² and rearrange for the horizontal acceleration.
walkthrough: Horizontally, the particle starts from rest and moves 0.080 m in 0.64 s.
Use s = ½at²: 0.080 = ½a(0.64)².
The horizontal component of acceleration is 0.39 m s⁻².

ai_rubric.observable: Uses 0.080 = ½a(0.64)² for the horizontal motion.
Obtains a horizontal acceleration of 0.39 m s⁻².

parts.label: (e)(i)
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the electric field strength.

parts.label: (e)(ii)
parts.text: The sand particle has mass $m$ and charge $q$. Use your answers in (d) and (e)(i) to determine the ratio $\frac{q}{m}$.

markscheme_points.text: ma = Eq or F = ma and F = Eq

marking_points.text: ma = Eq or F = ma and F = Eq

parts.label: (f)(i)
parts.part_stem:
Another particle has a smaller magnitude of the ratio $\frac{q}{m}$ than the sand particle. This particle is also released from point X.

For the movement of this particle, state the effect, if any, of the decreased magnitude of the ratio on:
parts.text: the vertical component of the acceleration

parts.label: (f)(ii)
parts.text: the horizontal component of the acceleration.

hints: For a uniform field between parallel plates, relate field strength to the potential difference divided by the plate separation.
Convert 900 V and 0.12 m using E = ΔV / d.
walkthrough: For a uniform field between parallel plates, E = ΔV / d.
The potential difference is 900 V and the separation is 0.12 m.
The electric field strength is 7.5 × 10³ N C⁻¹.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses E = ΔV / d for the uniform field.
Calculates the field strength as 7.5 × 10³ N C⁻¹.

hints: The horizontal electric force produces the horizontal acceleration, so equate the two force expressions.
From ma = Eq, cancel m and divide by E before substituting the results from (d) and (e)(i).
walkthrough: The horizontal electric force is Eq and the horizontal resultant force is ma.
Equating them gives ma = Eq.
Cancel m and rearrange: q / m = a / E.

ai_rubric.observable: Equates the horizontal forces as ma = Eq, or states both F = ma and F = Eq.
Uses q / m = 0.39 / (7.5 × 10³) and obtains 5.2 × 10⁻⁵ C kg⁻¹.

hints: The electric field acts horizontally, whereas the particle's weight acts vertically.
A change in q / m changes only the electric acceleration component, so consider whether the vertical force has changed.
walkthrough: The electric force is horizontal, so it affects only the horizontal component of acceleration.
The vertical force is the particle's weight, which is unchanged when q / m decreases.
Therefore the vertical component of acceleration is unchanged: there is no effect.

ai_rubric.observable: States that the decreased magnitude of q / m has no effect on the vertical component of acceleration.

hints: The electric field strength is unchanged, so compare only the charge-to-mass ratio in the horizontal acceleration relationship.
Combine F = ma with F = Eq to express horizontal acceleration in terms of q / m and E.
walkthrough: The horizontal electric force is Eq, so ma = Eq.
Thus the horizontal acceleration is a = (q / m)E.
With the field strength unchanged, a smaller magnitude of q / m gives a smaller horizontal acceleration.
Therefore the horizontal component of acceleration decreases.

ai_rubric.observable: States that the horizontal component of acceleration decreases, or is smaller.
